sections.overview: The large white is a big white butterfly of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, a strong flier and migrant. Its caterpillars feed in groups on cabbage-family plants, making it a well-known garden and crop pest.
sections.identification: Wingspan is about 58–63 mm in one source and 63–70 mm in another. The wings are white with black forewing tips extending down the edge; females have two black forewing spots and a hindwing spot, which males lack. The underside is creamy white. The caterpillar is yellowish green with black spots, and its eggs are yellow and skittle-shaped. The consulted species references do not provide a reliable adult body mass for identification; no weight is estimated here.
sections.habitat: It breeds mainly in gardens, allotments and farmland where cabbages grow, and adults also visit meadows, heaths, parks and woodland rides. It occurs across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia as far as the Himalayas, and was accidentally introduced to Chile.
sections.diet: Caterpillars eat mainly cultivated cabbage, Brussels sprouts and oilseed rape, and also nasturtium, wild mignonette and sea-kale. Young caterpillars feed communally, starting with the outer leaves, and the species is a well-known cabbage pest.
sections.behavior: The species is a strong flier and strongly migratory: migrants from continental Europe often reach Britain in spring and autumn, adding to the resident population. Fully grown caterpillars wander away from the food plant to pupate, often under windowsills, eaves, fences or tree trunks.
sections.reproduction: Females lay yellow eggs in batches of typically 20 to 60 under cabbage leaves, hatching in about ten days. In Britain adults emerge from April, with one or sometimes two further broods, and they fly until mid-September. Chrysalises of the last brood overwinter.
sections.ecology: Caterpillars accumulate mustard oils from their food plants, which make them unpalatable to most predators and birds. The wasp Apanteles glomeratus parasitises young caterpillars, reportedly killing a large share of them, and Pteromalus puparum attacks freshly formed pupae.
sections.conservation: In Great Britain it is rated Least Concern (2022 Red List) and its European status is not threatened. Even so, UK monitoring shows abundance down 32% between 1976 and 2019 and distribution down 18% between 1973 and 2019.
